lines.text: Dilli… CSE?
Mera Durgapur aaya. Kajal ka Dilli!
lines.en: I got Durgapur. Kajal got Delhi!

lines.text: Mumma, I got NIT Delhi!
Meet Shalini. She lives in a village in Saharsa district, in north Bihar. Her twin brother is Sonu.
Kajal lives in Begusarai, a town. Her twin brother is Kundan.
And Ira lives in Patna, the state capital. Her twin brother is Vivaan.
All six took the JEE and got the same rank, 8,000. All three girls got a seat at NIT Delhi, in computer science. All three boys got NIT Durgapur.
Same rank. Same seat. Which of the three girls actually goes to Delhi? Make a guess, and keep it. We'll come back to it.

First, is there a gap at all? Some Indian families draw a circle around a daughter, about 100 kilometres from home, and she studies inside it. Her brother gets no such circle. We wanted to put numbers on that.
Take every student in the 2011 Census who moved to study. Each time the distance of the move doubles, the odds that the student is a woman fall by about 9 per cent.

But maybe the girls who moved had lower marks? Maharashtra lets us check. At the same entrance score, women are 3.7 points less likely to study outside their home region. That's about one in seven fewer.
Why does it happen? The direct test would be the choice lists: which colleges each girl and boy actually put down. We asked for them under the RTI Act. The reply: not readily available.

So we built a model. Think of it as a calculator. You put in seats, pay, fares and travel times, and it tells you what families would choose. Every number from here on comes out of it, not from a survey.
Start with the textbook. In the standard model, from the economist Gary Becker, a family invests in a child's education like any other investment. Nothing in it depends on gender.
Same rank, same return, same price. So, the same college.
Ability? Same rank. Price? Same ticket. Girls prefer home? That isn't an answer. It's what we're explaining.
And here's the twist. At the same rank, the sister has the better seat. The women-only pool gets Kajal into NIT Delhi. Kundan's best is NIT Durgapur.
Median starting pay at NIT Delhi is 15.4 lakh rupees a year. At Durgapur, 11. A lakh is a hundred thousand rupees.
So by the textbook, she should go further than her brother. Often, she doesn't.

So how does our model work? Picture the parents at choice filling. From last year's closing ranks, they know which seats the twins can get. Now they decide what to put first. There are four ways to send the twins.
One: both stay at NIT Patna, close to home.
Two, together: both go to Durgapur, his college.
Three, best seats: he takes Durgapur, she takes Delhi.
Four: only he goes. He takes Durgapur, and she stays at Patna.
Each option gets a score, like weighing it on a scale. On one side is the value: his pay plus her pay after the degree, counted for their first three years of work.
On the other side are the costs. There are two of them, and only the daughter carries them.
Akeli kaise jayegi? Babuji jayenge saath mein.
lines.en: How will she go alone? Babuji will go with her.

lines.text: Cost one is money. Sonu travels alone. Shalini doesn't. Her father goes with her, and loses about four days of farm work on every trip, at 379 rupees a day.
Add up four years of fares for both children, her father's tickets and his lost days. For Shalini's family, it comes to about 62 thousand rupees.
Now compare: one year of Delhi's extra pay over Patna is 6.4 lakh. The whole bill is less than a tenth of that. So if the family says no, it isn't the ticket.
Cost two is worry. Her parents worry for every hour it would take them to reach her if something went wrong.
From Shalini's village: an auto to Saharsa Junction. 24 hours on the Vaishali Express. Then a cab across Delhi. Door to door, 26 and a half hours.
Dono saath jaoge. Kundan rahega na saath.
lines.en: You'll both go together. Kundan will be with you.

lines.text: Akeli Dilli? Log kya kahenge?
lines.en: Delhi, alone? What will people say?

lines.text: That worry has two parts. One is a belief about a place they have never seen. Facts can move it.
The other is log kya kahenge: what will people say. No fact moves that.
Economists call the first statistical discrimination, and the second, taste.
Now see why together is so cheap. Put the twins in one college, and the brother becomes the escort, and someone who's there. Both costs fall at once. The son himself carries neither.
Economists call her the tied mover: she moves for someone else's best option. Mincer used it for wives who move for a husband's job.
So the score is value, minus money, minus worry. Let's work it out for Shalini.
Best seats has the most value: 79 lakh, against 66 for together. Money takes off almost nothing.
But Delhi is 26 and a half hours away, so its worry is big: 22 lakh. Durgapur is closer, and Sonu is there, so its worry is only about 7.
Net, together scores 58. Best seats, 55 and a half. Together wins, but only just.
Here is the whole model on one page. Four lines.
Value: his pay plus her pay, counted for three years.
Money: the fares, her father's tickets and his lost days, weighted by how much a rupee hurts that family. A poor family feels each rupee more.

Worry: the hours it takes to reach her, times how much each hour worries them. The part about the place shrinks with every girl from home who went before, and when her brother is there. Log kya kahenge doesn't shrink.
Score: value, minus money, minus worry. For the son, there is no escort and no worry. That's the whole model. Everything else is an input.
But a score isn't a choice. So what does out of 100 mean?
Picture 100 families exactly like Shalini's. Same rank, same village, same fares.
They still differ in things we can't see. A cousin in Durgapur. A pushy uncle. A bad dream.
So they don't all choose alike. When two scores are close, families split nearly half and half. When one score is far ahead, almost all of them pick it.
Kajal's family scores 60.4 for together and 60.5 for best seats, so they split almost evenly. Ira's best seats is 12 points ahead, so nearly every Ira goes.
Now, your guess. Out of 100 Shalinis, 23 take Delhi. 59 go with Sonu to Durgapur. 14 stay at Patna while Sonu leaves. And in 4, both stay.
Out of 100 Kajals, 44 take Delhi, and 42 go with Kundan.
Out of 100 Iras, 98 take Delhi.
So the city girl gets her wish. The town girl is on the fence. And the village girl, with the longest trip, mostly goes where her brother goes.
Where does Shalini's 23 come from? Add the costs one at a time.
If only pay counted, 99 Shalinis in 100 would take Delhi. Add the fares and her escort: still 98.
Add the worry about a place they can't see: 39. Add log kya kahenge: 23. The worry does almost all the work.
Now ask a simpler question: who leaves Bihar at all? The brothers: 96, 98 and 100 times in 100. The sisters: 82, 86 and 100.
Shalini's 82 is the 23 who take Delhi, plus the 59 who go with Sonu.
So in Bihar the gap mostly isn't she stays home. It's she goes where her brother goes.
And going with her brother has a price. NIT Delhi's median pay is 15.38 lakh, Durgapur's 11.01. So a sister who goes with him gives up about 4.4 lakh a year.
Her father isn't being cruel. He's buying something: a free escort, and someone who's there.
These are the parents' choices. But what if Shalini has a say?
In a standard bargaining model, she gets Delhi once her say is at least 0.3, on a scale of 0 to 1.
In Patna, Ira's parents want Delhi too, so there is nothing to argue about.
But whose limit is it? Our professor asked us exactly that. Is it only the parents', or does she feel unsafe too?
We asked five women from our own circles. For three, the limit was only the family's. One shared the worry, about some places, not about distance. And one went far, on a joint decision.
Five calls are a pilot, not a sample. But both cases exist. If she wants to go, information for her parents helps. If she's afraid too, only a safer trip does.
How far should you trust these numbers? Let's be honest about what goes in.
Pay, seats and the main fares are sourced.

One number, the size of the worry, we set ourselves. We set it so that Kajal's family sits on the fence. So her 44 is by design. It is not a finding. Shalini's 23 and Ira's 98 then follow from the model.
How many years of pay the family counts, the split of the worry, and how much families differ are assumed.
And the order of the three girls doesn't depend on those guesses. It follows the trip.
Ira's parents can reach her in under 6 hours, by air. Kajal's, in 21. Shalini's, in 26 and a half.
Now look at Ira. Her family spends the most on travel, about 1.65 lakh rupees over four years. She still takes Delhi, because Delhi is one flight away: under six hours, door to door.
Her parents' one worry is the last leg: 48 kilometres across Delhi, in a cab, alone. We found no safety data for that road, so the model can't put a number on it.
The worry also feeds itself. No senior girl from her district at the college, so nobody to call, so not safe for girls, so no senior girl next year either.
So let's test some fixes. With a model, you change one input and run it again.
Pay her father's tickets: Shalini's 23 becomes 26.
Put one senior girl from her district at NIT Delhi: 85. Promise every first-year girl a hostel place, and publish campus safety data: also 85. Both: 96.
Why so big? A senior girl is someone her parents can call. A hostel promise works the same way. Both shrink the part of the worry that facts can move, and they break the loop.
Money barely moves her. Information does.
The size rests on an assumed worry split. The ranking doesn't.
And NIT Delhi does have a girls' hostel. What our fix adds is a promise: a place for every first-year girl, told to her family before they fill their choices.
Is that only our model? We asked five women what would have made a far college OK. Three gave the same answer: a relative in that city.
One told us her family said no to Bombay, and yes to Delhi, because her grandparents lived there. That's our senior-girl fix, in a real family.
Every model breaks somewhere. Here is where ours does.
One. The three families are composites, not real people. Twins are a device to hold the rank fixed.
Two. Without the choice lists, we can't test the gap at the moment families choose.
Three. The levels move with our assumptions. Count one year of pay instead of three, and Shalini's Delhi chance is 1 in 100. Count five, and it's 88. But the order of the girls never changes.
Four. One prediction worked: in Maharashtra, the gap closes for toppers.
And one failed. Colleges far from an airport don't have more empty seats for women.
And the Census pattern is a link, not proof of a cause. So we say goes with, never causes.
So, three things to remember.
One. At the same rank, the sister often has the better seat.
Two. What holds her back isn't the fare. It's worry, and it grows with every hour of the trip.
Three. Information moves her far more than money.
Now you decide. In our game, choose for a family, and see what it costs.
